events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Sam proposes Sam, Noah. With five players and a two-person mission one team, there is no information yet that justifies excluding anyone. I include myself (Sam) to signal that I will take a risk and share responsibility for the mission outcome rather than stacking the team on others, and I pair myself with Noah. A two-player good team on mission one still leaves three others unselected, so I would rather test an untested configuration with people I have no reason to suspect than to imply a suspicion without evidence.

I support Sam's proposed team of Sam and Noah. Mission 1 has no public signal, and the proposal is a reasonable two-player test: it keeps the team small, gives us a clean result, and avoids overcommitting before we have evidence. I have no specific objection to either Sam or Noah at this point. I would rather see this team voted through than spend a rejection on speculation.

I think Sam's team of Sam and Noah is reasonable for mission one. There is no prior information to work with, so the leader has little to go on beyond personal judgment. Including himself as leader on a two-person team is a fair signal — he is putting himself at equal risk rather than pushing the mission onto others. Noah has no public record against him either. I do not see a strong reason to reject this, and spending our first rejection on a team like this would set a bad precedent. Let us vote it through and learn from the outcome.

I am on this proposed team with Sam, and I support it. Mission one has no information to work from, so I agree with Leo and Arjun that rejecting a reasonable proposal now would waste a rejection and set a bad precedent. Sam including himself as leader is a fair accountability signal, and I have nothing in my own read of the table that raises concern about either of us. If this team passes, I will play a Success card, and the result will give us a genuine data point about both Sam and me going forward. One thing I would like to hear before we vote: Omar, you are the only player who has not weighed in yet — do you see any reason to reject this team that the rest of us have missed, or are you comfortable letting it go to a vote as proposed?

Noah, to answer your question directly: I have not rejected this team, and I see no reason to. Mission one has no public information, and Sam including himself as leader is a reasonable signal. Sam and Noah are a clean two-person test with no evidence against either of them. I was listening to the discussion before speaking, and I am comfortable letting this team go to a vote as proposed.

Thank you, Leo, Arjun, Noah, and Omar — that is a clear consensus, and it is enough for me to go to the vote with the team exactly as proposed: Sam and Noah.

Let me restate the reasoning once so the record is clean. This is mission one. There is no public information about anyone's role and no failed mission to read. The only signal available is judgment, and the reasonable thing to do with no information is to build the smallest team the mission allows and choose players I have no specific reason to doubt. I include myself deliberately: I would rather carry the same risk as my teammate than stack the burden on someone else and hide behind my position as leader. If this team fails, I am one of the two who failed, and I accept that.

Noah is on this team, and his read has been open and consistent with everyone else's — he asked whether anyone saw a reason to reject, and when Omar answered directly with none, the discussion closed without friction. That kind of behavior is worth noting early, because how people behave before there is anything to hide tends to carry forward.

I am not going to over-argue this or pretend I have insights I do not have. There is nothing in front of me that justifies a different team, and spending our first rejection on a speculative exclusion would cost us the ability to make an evidence-based rejection later when a rejection actually matters. If Sam and Noah succeed, we learn a little about both of us. If they fail, we get our first real data point and can build a team on something other than guesswork.

I am keeping the team as Sam and Noah, and I ask the table to vote it through so we can start learning.

I agree with the team as proposed: Sam and Noah. Nothing from the discussion points to a better choice, and a rejection now would spend a team without any evidence against either player. Sam's willingness to share the risk and Noah's direct answers have been consistent so far. I will vote to approve and see what the result tells us.

Short and final from me: the team stands as Sam and Noah, and I am ready to put it to the vote.

We have now heard from every player, and there is no disagreement to resolve. Leo, Arjun, Noah, and Omar each independently read the same thing — no information, no accusation, and a leader who put himself on the mission rather than distributing risk. That unanimity on mission one is worth recording, because it means the table has set its own baseline for how we reason with no evidence, and we should hold ourselves to that baseline when evidence does arrive.

Two things I want on the record about why I am not changing the team. First, I am a Loyal Servant and I want a successful mission; there is no reading of this table in which I gain anything by weakening a team that nobody has reason to doubt. Second, the cost of a rejection here is concrete: we would spend a rejection on a hunch and lose the ability to make an evidence-based rejection later when one actually matters, and if we rejected repeatedly and the same team kept succeeding, we would hand the game to Evil without ever learning anything.

If Sam and Noah succeed, we learn that two players I chose without suspicion are likely good, and we build from there. If they fail, we get our first real data point and can reason about what actually happened instead of about how people sounded in a discussion where everyone behaved the same way.

I am not asking anyone for anything further, and I am not going to keep talking past the point where it helps. The team is Sam and Noah. Please vote.

I agree with the consensus — Sam and Noah is a sound team for mission one. Every player has now weighed in, and there is no friction to resolve. Sam putting himself on the team is a fair accountability signal, and Noah's read has been open throughout the discussion. I have no reason to object to either player, and rejecting now would spend a rejection without evidence behind it. The team as proposed gives us a clean baseline to reason from. I am ready to vote it through and see what mission one tells us.

Final word from me, and then I will stop.

The team stands as Sam and Noah, unchanged. Every player has spoken, every player has independently reached the same read, and there is no unresolved point left for me to address. Leo, Arjun, Noah, and Omar each said the same thing in their own words: no information on mission one, no reason to doubt either player, and no reason to spend our first rejection on a hunch. That is the whole case, and it is enough.

I want to be honest about what my proposal actually is, rather than dressing it up. It is not a clever read. It is the default choice given no evidence, and the only content in it is that I put myself on the mission instead of distributing the risk to two people whose behavior I had not yet observed. If this fails, I fail with the team. That is the accountability signal, and I think it is the right one to establish on mission one: from here on, any criticism of my judgment should come with better information than I had today, not just better rhetoric.

There is also a strategic cost to rejecting. If we reject a reasonable team now, we spend the rejection on a hunch and lose the ability to reject for a real reason later. If we kept rejecting while the same players kept succeeding, we would be handing the game to Evil without ever learning anything useful. I would rather gather a genuine data point from a clean mission and reason from what actually happens.

I expect this mission to succeed, and I say that not because I know anything, but because there is no reading of this table in which a Loyal Servant gains anything by weakening a team that nobody has reason to doubt. When the result comes back, the useful information will be who was on the mission and whether it held, nothing about how anyone sounded in a discussion where everyone behaved identically. I will hold myself to that standard of evidence as the game moves on, and I will expect it of the rest of the table as well.

The team is Sam and Noah. I am ready to put it to the vote and I am not asking anyone for anything further.

The team stands as Sam and Noah, and I fully support it going to a vote as proposed. I am one of the two on this mission, and I want to be plain about what that means: I will play a Success card, and I have every expectation the result will be a Success. Sam has conducted this proposal cleanly — he put himself at risk rather than distributing it, he kept the team unchanged once consensus formed, and he has not over-argued a position that did not need arguing. The table reached the same read independently: no evidence exists yet, mission one is a data-gathering exercise, and rejecting a team nobody has raised a specific concern about would waste our first rejection on a hunch. I have nothing to hide about my role or my intentions on this mission. If it succeeds, Sam and I both gain credibility; if it somehow fails, we are both directly implicated and the table should weight that accordingly. I have heard no objection from Leo, Arjun, or Omar, and no new point has been raised in the later turns that changes the picture. I am ready to vote and see the result give us something real to reason from.

I have made my position clear, so I will keep this short. I am approving Sam and Noah as proposed. Nothing in the discussion gives a reason to reject, and a rejection now would spend a team without evidence. I am ready for the vote, and I will judge the team by what the mission result shows.

I will keep this brief since I have already stated my position, and nothing new has been raised since. The team stands as Sam and Noah, and I support it going to a vote. I am one of the two on this mission, I will play a Success card, and I expect a successful result. No one at this table — Leo, Arjun, Sam, or Omar — has raised a specific concern about either member, and spending our first rejection on a team with no evidence against it would cost us the ability to reject for a real reason later. The discussion has reached its natural end: every player has endorsed this proposal, the leader has declined to revise it, and there is no unresolved point worth another turn. If the mission succeeds, Sam and I both gain credibility. If it fails, we are both directly implicated, and the table should weight that accordingly. I am ready for the vote.

I still support the proposed team of Sam and Noah. Mission 1 has no public signal, and this is a clean two-person test: Sam included himself as leader, and Noah has answered directly without any specific concern being raised against him. Rejecting now would spend a rejection without evidence, and I would rather see the mission result than infer suspicion from discussion alone. I have no specific objection to either Sam or Noah, and I am ready to vote to approve this team as proposed.

Sam confirms Sam, Noah. The discussion closed with unanimous support: Leo, Arjun, Noah, and Omar each independently reached the same read, and no specific concern was raised against either Sam or Noah. Mission one offers no public information, so there is nothing to justify spending our first rejection on a hunch, and doing so would cost us the ability to make an evidence-based rejection later. Sam's inclusion of himself was deliberate — I take the same risk as my teammate rather than distributing the burden to players whose behavior I have not yet observed. I am keeping the lineup of Sam and Noah unchanged and am ready to put it to the vote.
Team approved (5 approve, 0 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Omar proposes Omar, Arjun, Leo. Mission 1 succeeded with Sam and Noah, so I want to test players who have not yet been on a mission. I include myself as leader to share the risk, and I pair Arjun and Leo, who have no mission record yet. This keeps the team at the required three without relying on the proven pair.

I am on this proposed team, so I want to be clear: I will play Success. But I do not support this lineup as proposed. Mission 1 gave us exactly one public data point: Sam and Noah completed a mission with zero fail cards. Omar's team contains neither of them. Instead it pairs Omar with Arjun and me, two players with no mission record. That is not automatically disqualifying, but it discards the only evidence we have and concentrates the proposal on untested players while leaving the successful pair off. With one fail enough on mission 2, I would rather add an untested player to at least one member of the successful mission, or at minimum not exclude both Sam and Noah. I ask Omar to revise the team to include one of Sam or Noah; if the slate is unchanged, I will vote against it.

Leo, that is a fair challenge, and I will not dismiss the Mission 1 result. Sam and Noah's clean success is the only public evidence we have. I am willing to revise the team so that Noah replaces you: Omar, Arjun, and Noah. That keeps three players, includes one proven player, and still gives the untested players a chance to show their record. Leo, would you approve Omar, Arjun, and Noah if I revise to that? I would rather get a team approved than spend a rejection over one name. I will confirm the final slate after your answer.

Omar, to answer your question directly: no, I would not approve Omar, Arjun, and Noah. You replaced me with Noah, but the revised slate still contains two players with no mission record — you and Arjun — and only one member of the proven Sam/Noah pair. Mission 1 is our only public evidence: Sam and Noah produced a clean 0-fail result. With one fail enough on mission 2, I want both proven players on this mission, not just one. The cleanest revision is Sam, Noah, and Leo. I am on the original slate, I will play Success, and that lineup keeps the successful pair intact while testing one additional player. If you will not include both Sam and Noah, I will vote against the team. Omar, will you revise to Sam, Noah, and Leo and confirm that as the final slate?

Leo, to answer your question directly: no, I will not revise to Sam, Noah, and Leo, and I am keeping the slate as Omar, Arjun, and Leo. I already offered one revision in good faith to meet your concern about the proven pair, and you rejected it. Your objection is that the successful Sam and Noah pair should be kept together, but Mission 1 only tells us that two players with no fail cards completed a two-person mission. It does not show that they are the only trustworthy players at the table. Mission 2 is a three-person mission, and I would rather use it to test players who have no record yet than to repeat the same proven core and learn nothing new. Leo, you have said you will play Success, and I respect that. Arjun has also stated his intention to play Success, and the team is balanced enough to give us real information either way. If this mission succeeds, we have three clean results and a clearer picture of everyone on the table. If it fails, we have our first real data point about the people who were actually on it. I am not going to keep changing the team in response to each objection, because that spends discussion time without giving us evidence. The team is Omar, Arjun, and Leo. I ask the table to vote on it as proposed.

I will vote against Omar, Arjun, and Leo as proposed. I am on this slate and will play Success, but that does not make the lineup sound. The only public evidence we have is Mission 1: Sam and Noah completed a clean 0-fail mission. Omar's final slate excludes both proven players and places two players with no mission record, Omar and Arjun, alongside me. With one fail enough on Mission 2, that is the riskiest possible use of our only evidence. Omar already refused the good-faith revision to include one proven player, then refused the cleaner Sam, Noah, Leo lineup. I understand the argument that repeating a proven core teaches less, but an unproven three-person team does not teach us more safely; it simply gives Evil a better chance to fail the mission. I have no specific public accusation beyond that, but my vote is no. If this is rejected, I will support a team that includes at least one, and preferably both, of Sam and Noah, with the remaining slot used to test someone new.

I support the team Omar, Arjun, and Leo, and I will vote to approve it. Leo, I want to push back directly on your objection, because I think it overstates what Mission 1 actually told us. Sam and Noah played a two-person mission and returned zero fail cards. That is a clean result, but it is a narrow one: it tells us those two passed one test with one fail threshold, not that they are the only credible players at this table. You are asking us to treat one data point as a permanent shield for two names, and to treat every other player — Omar, me, you — as permanently suspect by comparison. That is not evidence-based reasoning; it is caution that has hardened into a default.

Omar already offered a good-faith revision by including Noah, and you rejected it while demanding the full Sam, Noah, Leo slate. Notice what that demand does: it locks the mission around the same two names every time, so we never learn anything about the rest of us. Missions are how Good builds evidence. If we only ever send the proven pair, we gather no new information and Evil gets to hide behind a shrinking list of trusted players. A three-person mission with Omar, Arjun, and Leo is a fair test. If it succeeds, three more players have clean records and the picture widens. If it fails, the three of us on the mission are directly implicated and we will know exactly where to look.

I have no reason to suspect Omar. His original team was a reasonable attempt to test unproven players, he revised once in good faith, and he has been transparent about his reasoning. Leo, your insistence on excluding everyone outside the Mission 1 pair is the only friction at this table, and it is friction based on a single result. I ask the table to judge the team on its merits: three willing players, no specific accusation against any of them, and a result that will give us more information than repeating the same two names would.

I am voting yes on Omar, Arjun, and Leo.

Leo, I have heard your objection and want to answer the specific point you raised: that Mission 1 is our only evidence. A two-person mission with zero fail cards shows that Sam and Noah passed one test. It does not show that the other three of us are untrustworthy, and repeating that same pair would teach the table nothing about the rest of us. I already offered a good-faith revision to include Noah, and I will not keep reshaping the slate every time someone objects. You have said you will play Success, so the risk you describe is one you can resolve by approving this team. Rejecting it spends one of our five rejections, and the team you would be voting against includes you. Arjun and I have both committed to Success as well. If the three of us are the Good players you believe we are, the mission will show it. I ask you to vote to approve Omar, Arjun, and Leo.

I support the team as proposed: Omar, Arjun, and Leo. I want to be plain that I am not doing this because I have read anyone at this table — I have not. I am doing it because the evidence available does not support spending a rejection.

First, what Mission 1 actually showed. Sam and Noah completed a two-person mission with zero fail cards. That is one clean result on one narrow test, and I was one of the two people it happened to. It does not tell us that Omar, Arjun, or Leo are untrustworthy, and Leo's own reasoning overstates it: he is asking the table to treat a single result as a permanent shield for two names, and to treat the other three of us as permanently suspect by comparison. Caution that hardens into a default is not evidence-based reasoning, it is just caution. I recognize his concern about risk on a one-fail mission is real and legitimate — that is exactly the concern Arjun and Omar are answering, not dismissing.

Second, the information argument. If Omar, Arjun, and Leo go out and the mission fails, we have our first real data point and we know precisely which three names to examine. If it succeeds, three more players have clean records and our picture of the table widens. If we only ever send the proven pair, we never learn anything about the rest of us, and Evil gets to hide behind a list that keeps shrinking. Every mission we spend on the same names is a mission Evil is happy with.

Third, the cost. A rejection here spends one of our five rejections on a single narrow data point, moves leadership, and produces no new information about anyone. It is a real price for a real but unproven benefit. Leo says he will play Success and is on this slate himself; I have heard no specific accusation against Omar or Arjun beyond the absence of a record. Absence of a record is not evidence of guilt, and I will not treat it as such.

One thing I want on the record for myself: my Mission 1 success does not make me a safer bet than anyone else, and I do not want the table reasoning as though it does. I would rather be judged by what the missions show than by what one lucky pair did once.

Noah, you are the player whose record Leo is asking us to keep on missions, so I want to hear your view on the specific point rather than guess at it: do you want to be on Mission 2, and do you think Leo's objection is strong enough to justify spending a rejection here?

Sam asked me two direct questions, so I will answer both plainly. First: do I want to be on Mission 2? I am willing to serve if the table sends me, and I would play Success on any team I am on. But I do not require a seat, and I will not spend a rejection to get one. A mission that includes me is not automatically safer than one that does not, and I will not let my own preference distort the table's read of the evidence. Second: is Leo's objection strong enough to justify spending a rejection here? No, and I want to be precise about why. Leo's argument is that Mission 1 is our only public evidence, and that a team containing neither Sam nor me discards it entirely. But look at what actually happened in this discussion. Omar offered a revision — Omar, Arjun, and me — that included one member of the proven pair. Leo rejected that revision and demanded both Sam and me, plus himself. That is no longer an argument about evidence; it is a demand for a specific lineup. If the concern were genuinely 'at least one proven player,' Omar's revision answered it, and Leo's refusal of it tells us the standard keeps moving. The table cannot operate on a standard that no revision can satisfy. I also want to push back on what Mission 1 actually proves, since I was on it. Sam and I completed a two-person mission with zero fail cards. That is a genuine data point, but it is a narrow one: two players passed one small test. It does not make Sam and me a permanent shield, and it does not make Omar, Arjun, or Leo suspect by comparison. Leo says a three-person team of unproven players is 'the riskiest possible use of our only evidence.' I disagree — Leo himself is on that slate and has committed to Success, and Omar and Arjun have both been transparent and reasonable in this discussion. Absence of a mission record is not evidence against anyone. There is also the information cost of Leo's position. If we accept that every mission must contain both Mission 1 members, then Mission 2 is Sam, me, and one rotating seat, and the other three players stay permanently untested. That is exactly the pattern Evil benefits from: a shrinking trusted core, no new data, and every rejection spent protecting the status quo. If Omar, Arjun, and Leo go and it succeeds, three more players have clean records. If it fails, we know precisely which three names to examine. Either result teaches us more than repeating the same pair. I support Omar, Arjun, and Leo as proposed, and I will vote to approve. Leo, you said after a rejection you would support a team with at least one of Sam and me — but Omar already offered you exactly that, and you turned it down. I see no reason to reject a team that includes

I have spoken once already on this proposal, so let me be brief and add only what is new.

Leo's objection has now been fully tested and it has not produced a workable team. The standard he applied was not "at least one proven player" — it was "both Sam and Noah, plus Leo." Omar offered the first version and Leo turned it down. Leo's own words are that after a rejection he would support a team with at least one of us on it, and he then refused exactly that. That is not an evidentiary standard; it is a demand for a specific lineup, and no leader can meet it. A rejection here would therefore not be a vote against a bad team; it would be a vote to transfer leadership to someone who can write Leo's preferred slate, and it would spend one of our five rejections to do it.

On the evidence itself, nothing has changed since my last turn and I want to correct one point rather than restate my position. My Mission 1 success with Noah does not make us safer bets than anyone else, and Leo's reasoning treats us as though it does. One two-person mission with a one-fail threshold is a narrow result. It does not make Omar, Arjun, or Leo suspect by comparison, and absence of a record is not evidence of guilt. If anything, my own record should make me wary of the pattern Leo is defending — a shrinking trusted core, every new player permanently untested, and a rejection spent defending that list instead of gathering information.

On the risk: Leo is on this slate himself and has stated plainly that he will play Success. Omar and Arjun have committed to Success as well, and they have been transparent throughout this discussion. If Evil is among these three, this mission exposes them immediately and precisely, and we learn exactly where to look. If Evil is among the untested three, then a slate built around Sam and Noah would simply have hidden them again, and we would have learned nothing. Either way the information is better, and the risk is one that the people carrying it have already accepted.

The cost of saying no is concrete and the benefit is speculative. Rejecting buys no new information, spends a rejection, and moves the proposal to a leader whose next slate will be built to satisfy Leo's condition. Approving buys us a real data point on three players.

Omar, Arjun, and Leo is the team. I support it, I will vote to approve it, and I do not think the evidence supports spending our first rejection here.

Sam, your last turn actually helps Omar's case more than it helps yours, and I want to say why plainly. You argue that no rejection should be spent because rejecting produces no new information — but you were the one on Mission 1, and your success there is the reason Leo can argue for a shrinking trusted core. You then say your record should not make you a safer bet. I agree. So does Leo's insistence on keeping both you and Noah on every mission follow from his own evidence? Mission 1 was a two-person team with a one-fail threshold. That is one narrow pass, not a permanent endorsement.

I want to address the table directly on the two points still in play. First, the so-called shifting standard. Omar offered Omar, Arjun, Noah — that satisfied 'at least one proven player.' Leo refused it and demanded both Sam and Noah plus himself. That is a lineup demand, not an evidentiary standard, and no leader can meet it without excluding players who deserve testing. Noah himself said it: if every mission must include both Mission 1 members, the other three stay permanently untested and Evil hides behind a shrinking list.

Second, the risk. The team Omar, Arjun, Leo contains Leo, who has publicly committed to Success. Omar has committed. I have committed. Three named players, all of whom have been transparent, all of whom accept direct accountability if the mission fails. The threshold is one fail. If Evil is sitting on this slate, the mission exposes them precisely. If Evil is among Sam, Noah, or Omar, a slate built around the Mission 1 pair would simply hide them again.

Leo, I have heard your objection twice now and it has not moved. If your real concern is accountability, this slate gives you more of it than any alternative — you are on it. If your concern is that only Sam and Noah can be trusted, that is a conclusion you reached from one two-person pass and are now applying as a rule. I am voting yes on Omar, Arjun, and Leo, and I ask the table to approve it so we can get a real data point instead of spending a rejection to protect a two-name list.

Arjun, you have answered the point I raised, and I want to be clear that your reading of it is correct — my Mission 1 success is not a reason for the table to treat Sam and Noah as permanently safe, and the objection to the current slate has never rested on that. Leo's demand is the one the table has to price: after a good-faith revision that included one proven player, he rejected it and asked for a specific three-name lineup. That standard cannot be satisfied by any leader other than one who writes Leo's slate for them, so a rejection here does not buy a better team. It buys a rejection and a change of leadership.

I will not repeat my whole argument a third time; the substance is in the record. What I want to add is a note about what the outcome of this vote means for the rest of the game, since I do not want us to mistake this decision for a free one.

On risk: the three people on this slate — Omar, Arjun, Leo — have each publicly committed to playing Success, and each has accounted for the failure case in their own speech. The threshold on Mission 2 is one fail card. If Evil is among these three, the mission exposes them precisely and immediately, and we will know exactly where to look. If Evil is among the three who are not on it, a slate built around Sam and Noah would have hidden them again and we would have learned nothing. Either way, the information from approving is greater than the information from rejecting.

On cost: rejecting spends one of our five rejections, produces no new information about any player, and hands the next proposal to a leader whose slate is already predetermined. That is a real price for a speculative benefit, and we only have one rejection so far to spend on something we can actually point to.

On my own record, I want to be honest one more time, because I do not want the table reasoning from my success in a way I disagree with. Sam and Noah passing one two-person mission with one fail threshold is a narrow result. It is not a shield and I do not want it used as one. If the table's reasoning were 'protect the proven pair,' I would think that reasoning was soft, and I would say so whether or not it kept me off the mission. The team I am voting for is Omar, Arjun, and Leo, and I am voting yes on it for the reason that matters most: it is the slate that gives us a real data point about the table rather than repeating the one we already have.

I have said what I intend to say and I am ready to put the team to the vote.

We have now spent more time defending this team than any team deserves on mission two. The discussion has reached its natural conclusion, and I want to close it cleanly.

Let me state plainly what is actually at stake. Leo has objected twice. His objection rests on Mission 1 being our only evidence and the demand that both proven players stay on every mission. Omar already answered that objection by offering a revision with one proven player — Noah — and Leo refused it. Noah himself has said on the record that if every mission must include both Mission 1 members, the other three players stay permanently untested, and that is exactly the pattern Evil benefits from. That is the strongest argument in this discussion and it has not been answered.

The team Omar, Arjun, and Leo is a clean slate. Three players, all transparent, all committed to Success, all willing to accept direct accountability if the mission fails. If this mission succeeds, three more players have clean records and our picture of the table widens. If it fails, the three of us are directly implicated and the table knows exactly where to look. Either outcome teaches us more than protecting a two-name list from one narrow data point.

I am not asking Leo to change his mind. I am asking the rest of the table to vote yes so we can put this proposal to the ballot and get a real result instead of spending our first rejection on a position that no leader could satisfy.

The team is Omar, Arjun, and Leo. I support it and I am ready to vote.

Omar confirms Omar, Arjun, Leo. I'm keeping Omar, Arjun, and Leo. Mission 2 is a fresh test with three players who haven't been on a mission yet, and Sam and Noah have already produced our only public data point. Rejecting this slate would spend a rejection without new information.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 2 fails (2 fail cards).

Arjun proposes Arjun, Noah. Mission 3 requires a 2-player team. As leader I include myself (Arjun) to share risk openly, and pair with Noah, who has consistently supported proposals and voted to approve Mission 2. With one fail threshold, this gives me a seat to act on and keeps the proposal likely to pass the team vote.

I oppose Arjun and Noah. Mission 2 failed with two fail cards on a three-person team: Omar, Arjun, and me. I was on that mission and I played Success. That is the public reasoning I can offer: if I played Success, then both Omar and Arjun must have played Fail. I understand the table cannot verify my card, but the mission result and my statement are the only evidence we have, and they point directly at Arjun. Arjun is now leader and puts himself on Mission 3 alongside Noah. That is not a clean test; it gives one of the two players implicated by the failed mission another chance to fail, while attaching his risk to Noah's clean Mission 1 record. Noah should not be used to launder Arjun's record. I will vote against Arjun and Noah. If this team is rejected, the next leader should build Mission 3 from Sam, Noah, and players not implicated by Mission 2, and should not include Arjun or Omar. Noah, do you agree that being paired with Arjun, who was on the failed Mission 2, is enough reason to vote against this team?

Leo, I will answer your question directly, but not on the terms you set. The useful evidence here is not your claim about your own card — it is arithmetic. Mission 2 returned two fail cards from a three-person team. We are five players, so there are exactly two evil players at this table, and Good players must play Success. 2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
